title: Conversions in Real Situations
subtitle: Where a dropped zero actually costs something.
objectives: Apply volume conversions to practical problems
Work with mixed units in one problem
Judge whether an answer is physically sensible
Convert rates as well as amounts

cards.title: Same conversions, now with consequences
cards.text: In a test a wrong zero costs a mark. In a kitchen, a garage or a hospital it costs more than that.

cards.title: Get everything into one unit first
cards.text: Never calculate across two units. Convert, then work.
points: **Spot every unit** in the question before starting.
**Choose one** and convert everything to it.
**Then do the arithmetic.**
**Most mixed-unit errors** happen because someone skipped step one.

question.text: A jug holds 1.5 L. You pour in 400 mL. How much more fits?
question.explain: Convert first: 1.5 L is 1,500 mL. 1,500 − 400 = 1,100 mL.

cards.title: The same water, written in four units
cards.text: The same water in four units. Only the decimal point is moving.

cards.title: Water intake is a conversion problem
cards.text: Advice comes in litres. Bottles come in millilitres. The two have to meet.
points: **2 litres a day** is 2,000 mL.
**A 500 mL bottle** four times over.
**A 330 mL can** would take about six.
**Same amount**, different packaging.

question.text: A 2 L bottle is three-quarters full. How many mL is that? Digits only.
question.explain: 2 L is 2,000 mL. Three quarters of 2,000 is 1,500 mL.

cards.title: Convert the amount, keep the time
cards.text: A rate has two parts. Only one of them is changing.
points: **3 L per minute** is 3,000 mL per minute.
**The 'per minute' is untouched.**
**To change the time as well**, do it as a second step.
**One change at a time.**

cards.title: Working out if a fan suits a room
cards.text: The fan is rated in m³ per minute. The room is measured in metres. They already match.
points: **A 4 × 3 × 2.5 m room** is 30 m³.
**A fan moving 60 m³ a minute** turns that over twice a minute.
**No conversion needed**: both are already cubic metres.
**Matching units first** is half the work.

question.text: A tap runs at 12 L per minute. In millilitres per minute that is…
question.explain: Convert the amount only: 12 × 1,000 = 12,000 mL per minute. The 'per minute' does not change.

cards.title: Does the answer make physical sense?
cards.text: The last check is not arithmetic. It is whether the world would allow it.
points: **A glass holding 25 litres?** No.
**A bath holding 80 mL?** No.
**A wrong answer is usually a thousand out**, which is obvious once you look.
**Picture the object** before you write the number down.

cards.title: A flood warning is a conversion problem
cards.text: Dam levels come in metres, release rates in cubic metres per second. Both have to be read together.
points: **1 m³ per second** is 1,000 litres every second.
**A big release** is hundreds of times that.
**Per second matters**: an hour is 3,600 of them.
**The rate times the time** is what reaches the town.

terms.def: A problem stated in more than one unit.
An amount per unit of time, like litres per minute.
Asking whether an answer is physically possible.

cards.title: A real conversion, with a tap on it
cards.alt: A blue household water drum with a brass tap running into a bucket on the ground
cards.text: Litres in the drum, millilitres in the glass, cubic metres on the water bill.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Convert everything to one unit before calculating.
In a rate, convert the amount and leave the time alone.
A wrong answer here is usually out by exactly a thousand.
Picture the real object as your last check.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 8 Math, the second conversion week, moved from mechanics into use. The organising rule is convert-then-calculate, stated once and then enforced by every worked example, because mixed-unit arithmetic is where the marks actually go. Rates get their own card since converting both halves at once is a distinct and common error. The lesson closes on the sanity check, which is the most transferable habit in the whole topic: a wrong answer here is almost always out by exactly a thousand, and picturing the object catches it instantly.
discussion: Why convert before calculating rather than during?
In a rate, which part changes?
What is the fastest way to spot a factor-of-1,000 error?
extension: Work out how many bottles make up your daily water target.
Measure a room and work out how long a fan takes to turn its air over.
misconceptions: Converting both parts of a rate at once.
Not checking whether the answer is physically possible.
